::: {.kw-overview}
Prediction models wired into the electronic record dominate this fortnight. A pragmatic randomised trial at Vanderbilt found that acting on an autoimmune risk score after a positive ANA cut the median time to diagnosis from 138 to 43 days. A Mount Sinai delirium model held its discrimination when switched on at a second hospital without retraining, though most of its alerts were false positives. A Danish study of 2.08 million encounters adds a counterweight: across the whole population a machine learning early warning score barely improved on NEWS, and nearly all of its extra value sat in patients NEWS already rated as high risk. On large language models the theme is safety rather than capability. In a randomised trial, physicians who had completed AI-literacy training still lost 14 percentage points of diagnostic accuracy when ChatGPT-4o's suggestions contained planted errors. Twenty-four AI systems recommended care costing about three times what treating physicians ordered, and open-weight models used to grade clinical text missed one in ten clinical errors that experts caught. Two patient-facing tools close the issue: a 12-month trial found no mental health benefit from a generative AI maternal health chatbot, while a prospective study found that a consumer smartwatch picked up hypertension at least as well as a single office blood pressure reading.
:::

---

### 1. [Randomized Evaluation of an Autoimmune Disease Prediction Model - AURA (AUtoimmune Risk Assessment).](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2600112)
[Barnado A, Moore RP, Domenico HJ, Grace E, Green S, Suh A, Nikolova N, Han B, McCoy AB, Byrne DW. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42993025.]{.kw-ref}

Positive antinuclear antibody tests are common and most do not lead to autoimmune disease, yet there is no evidence-based way to decide who should see a rheumatologist quickly. This team at a single US academic health system built an interpretable prediction model into the electronic health record and ran a two-year pragmatic trial. Every patient with a new positive ANA was randomised 1:1 regardless of risk score. In the intervention arm, patients with high scores were invited for expedited rheumatology review. In the control arm, scores were calculated but not acted on, and both arms could be referred as usual. After post-randomisation exclusions, 954 intervention and 1,006 control patients were analysed from 2,385 randomised. Time from positive ANA to an autoimmune diagnosis was shorter with the model (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.3–2.7), and among those diagnosed the median was 43 days against 138. Among patients seen by rheumatology within six months, the proportion diagnosed was 23% versus 16%, which did not reach significance (P=0.07). The design cannot separate the model's contribution from that of the fast-track clinic it triggered, and the abstract reports no downstream clinical outcomes. For NHS rheumatology services facing long waits, it is one of the few randomised tests of an EHR risk score in routine care, but trusts would need to replicate it locally before using it to prioritise referrals.

### 2. [External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk.](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.42142)
[Friedman JI, Parchure P, Fu W, Cheertirala S, Timsina P, Raut G, Reina K, Joseph-Jimerson J, Mazumdar M, Freeman R, Reich DL, Kia A. *JAMA Netw Open*, 2026. PMID: 42981091.]{.kw-ref}

Delirium models often lose accuracy when moved to a new hospital, so this quality improvement study followed a multimodal model that includes natural language processing during live use for patients aged 60 and over on non-intensive care wards. The model was developed at Mount Sinai Hospital and switched on, without retraining, at Mount Sinai Morningside, with data from December 2024 to December 2025 covering 33,095 admissions. The two hospitals' patients differed in age, sex, ethnicity, surgical case mix, length of stay and dementia prevalence. Discrimination stayed high: the AUROC was 0.91 (95% CI 0.90–0.92) at the external hospital and 0.94 (0.93–0.94) at the development site. Positive predictive value was low, at 25.9% and 19.4% respectively, so most flagged patients did not develop recognised delirium. At the external hospital the mean monthly delirium detection rate roughly doubled after deployment, from 9.23% to 19.59%. That is a before-and-after comparison within one health system, and the post-deployment cohort was younger, so the gain cannot all be credited to the model. For NHS teams thinking about delirium screening tools, the useful lesson is that a model can travel between sites, but ward staff will need a plan for the large number of false alarms.

### 3. [Development and validation of early warning scores predicting 24 h mortality addressing intercurrent medical interventions in Denmark: a multicentre retrospective cohort study of 2·08 million hospital encounters.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landig.2026.101067)
[Katsiferis A, Scheidwasser N, Nguyen TL, Lange T, Khurana MP, Nielsen PB, Karmark Iversen K, Meyhoff CS, Kvanner Aasvang E, Mølgaard J, Zucco AG, Varga TV, Bhatt S. *Lancet Digit Health*, 2026. PMID: 42988715.]{.kw-ref}

This retrospective study used five years of records from 15 Danish hospitals (2,080,765 encounters from 825,200 adults) to ask whether anything beats NEWS at predicting death within 24 hours of the first score. NEWS was compared with two simpler rules (NEWS without blood pressure and temperature, and that version plus age and sex) and with XGB-EWS, a gradient-boosting model that adds laboratory results, demographics and text embeddings of medical history. Because high scores trigger treatment that can prevent the death being predicted, the authors used propensity weighting to reduce this intervention bias, and they judged models mainly by net benefit rather than discrimination alone. Across everyone, the gains were tiny: at most 1.9 extra correct identifications per 10,000 patients for XGB-EWS over NEWS, and 1.5 per 10,000 for NEWS over the simplified score. The picture changed when stratified by the first NEWS. In patients starting at 7 or above, XGB-EWS added up to 78.1 correct identifications per 10,000, while dropping blood pressure and temperature cost up to 60.2. For patients scoring 0–4, all the approaches performed almost identically. All validation was retrospective. For NHS trusts being offered EHR-based deterioration models to replace NEWS2, this suggests the case is strongest for the sickest patients and that a prospective, risk-stratified trial should come before wholesale replacement.

### 4. [Automation Bias in Large Language Model-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy - A Randomized Clinical Trial.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2501001)
[Qazi IA, Ali A, Khawaja AU, Akhtar MJ, Sheikh AZ, Alizai MH. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42932681.]{.kw-ref}

This single-blind randomised trial, run in Pakistan in mid-2025, tested whether AI-literacy training protects doctors from automation bias. Forty-four physicians completed a 20-hour training programme and were then randomised to work through six clinical vignettes with optional access to ChatGPT-4o diagnostic suggestions. The control group's suggestions were error-free; the intervention group's contained deliberate errors in three of the six cases, presented in random order. Physicians kept full control and could use their usual resources. Three blinded physicians scored a composite of differential diagnosis, supporting and opposing evidence, top diagnosis and next steps across 264 cases. Mean accuracy was 73.3% with the flawed suggestions against 84.9% with correct ones, an adjusted drop of 14.0 percentage points (95% CI −18.9 to −9.1). Accuracy for the top diagnosis fell from 90.5% to 76.1%, an adjusted difference of 18.3 points (95% CI −26.6 to −10.0). These were vignettes rather than real patients, the sample was small and from one country, and errors were planted at a fixed rate. For NHS organisations relying on training as the main safeguard for clinicians using chatbots, the trial suggests training alone does not stop doctors following a confident wrong answer.

### 5. [Comparative Cost of Care Recommended by Large Language Models versus Treating Physicians.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2600537)
[Aran D, Goldhaber-Fiebert JD, Many I, Nguyen A, Yang D, Shelly S. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42932470.]{.kw-ref}

The authors gave 24 AI systems the presenting history from 200 deidentified outpatient and emergency department notes in the public MTSamples collection and asked each to write a plan. The treating physician's documented plan was the comparator. Three separate language models extracted the orders, which were then priced at 2026 US Medicare rates for tests and specialist referrals, with new medicines counted rather than costed. Across the 20 general-purpose systems, recommended care averaged US$314 per visit against US$97 for physicians, a difference of US$216 (95% CI 177–257) or 3.2 times as much, split almost evenly between tests and referrals. The systems also proposed more new medicines (1.14 against 0.59 per visit), and the four medical-specialist systems were just as costly, at 2.7 to 3.5 times the physician figure. In the two-thirds of visits where the physician ordered no tests, every system still suggested some, usually a standard panel. Asking for cost awareness brought the ratio down to 2.5, and asking for a parsimonious but safe plan brought it to 1.4, but neither removed the excess. The comparator is what one physician documented, not a judgement of appropriate care, and US prices do not translate directly to the NHS. For UK clinicians using these tools to check a plan, the practical risk is reflexive over-investigation, which a carefully written prompt reduces but does not remove.

### 6. [Cross-paradigm audit of large language model judges for clinical text evaluation.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-026-03443-2)
[Pakull TMG, Warmer S, Arzideh K, Hilser T, Hosters B, Damm H, Nensa F, Schuler M, Borys K, Horn PA, Hosch R, Friedrich CM. *NPJ Digit Med*, 2026. PMID: 42982942.]{.kw-ref}

Health systems increasingly use one language model to grade the output of another, an approach called LLM-as-a-judge, but most of the evidence comes from English text and pooled agreement scores. This German team at University Hospital Essen tested six open-weight models as judges against expert panels on four German clinical datasets: report and nursing-note summaries, discharge summaries and patient letters. The models were tested across three evaluation formats and four prompt set-ups. Agreement with experts depended on the criterion and the dataset, and no set-up was reliable across formats. Every judge model showed position bias and identity bias. Replacing the experts with model judges changed 57.2% of category ratings, reversed 41.7% of head-to-head winners and missed 10.2% of the clinical errors the experts found. The models also gave too much weight to whether text was succinct and accurate, which reversed the experts' order of clinical priorities. The study covers German text and open-weight models only, and the abstract does not name the models. For NHS teams validating AI-written discharge summaries or letters, it suggests that automated grading cannot yet replace clinician review for safety checks.

### 7. [Generative Artificial Intelligence and Maternal Health Outcomes in Pregnant and Postpartum Individuals: A Randomized Clinical Trial.](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.41062)
[Norell EM, Yue X, Mane H, Marin Gutierrez FX, Srikanth NP, Smolyak D, Dipankar P, Peters CJ, Boyd-Graber J, Nguyen TT, He X, Nguyen QC. *JAMA Netw Open*, 2026. PMID: 42981095.]{.kw-ref}

This US trial recruited 400 pregnant or recently delivered participants online from 49 states, all from racial or ethnic minority groups. Half were randomised to a generative AI maternal health chatbot, Rosie, developed with community input, and half to an active control of a children's book posted each month. According to the full text, the chatbot sent automated alerts about distressing messages to a clinical social worker, who contacted the participant, and users were paid small sums per question to encourage engagement. At 12 months there was no difference in anxiety (adjusted GAD-7 difference 0.10, 95% CI −0.77 to 0.96) or depression (adjusted PHQ-9 difference −0.23, 95% CI −1.05 to 0.59). There was also no difference in emergency department visits, postpartum checks, contraception or sleep. Among those pregnant at enrolment, the chatbot group reported more pregnancy complications in one adjusted analysis (rate ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.02–1.92), a finding the longitudinal models did not support and that the authors call hypothesis-generating. Engagement was high, with a median of 119 questions per user, and heavier use went with longer sleep but higher anxiety scores, a non-randomised association that may reflect anxious users asking more. All outcomes were self-reported, the comparator was active, and baseline symptom scores were low. For NHS maternity services being offered conversational apps, this is a well-run negative trial, and it supports treating such tools as an adjunct to midwifery and perinatal mental health care, not a replacement.

### 8. [Opportunistically Detecting Signs of Hypertension on a Consumer Smartwatch.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11336-3)
[Di Achille P, Cai L, Wu J, Gao M, Daryani B, Wang J, Khanna U, Ko H, Pathak A, Malhotra M, Patel S, Shreibati JB, Juraschek SP, Rudrapatna P, Thompson M, Poh MZ. *Nature*, 2026. PMID: 42988369.]{.kw-ref}

This prospective multicentre study, by authors mostly from Google Research, tested an AI algorithm (AI-PPG-ACC-HTN) that reads photoplethysmography and accelerometer signals from a consumer smartwatch, with no cuff calibration, to flag possible hypertension. The 196 participants had no known cardiovascular disease and were not taking antihypertensives, and they wore the watch for seven days of normal life. The reference standard was 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. The algorithm detected hypertension with sensitivity 65.8% (95% CI 54.0–76.3%), specificity 90.0% (83.2–94.7%) and positive predictive value 80.6% (68.6–89.6%). By comparison, the initial office blood pressure screen had the same specificity but lower sensitivity, at 55.3% (43.4–66.7%), and a PPV of 77.8%. The confidence intervals overlap widely, so the claim is comparability rather than superiority. The sample is small, and about a third of people with hypertension were still missed. The authors present it as a prompt to get a cuff-based diagnosis, not a substitute for one. For UK GPs, this points to wearables as a case-finding nudge for people who never have their blood pressure checked, and a negative watch result should not be taken as reassurance.
